detailed_rationale:
Hindustan Zinc closed FY26 (year to March 2026) with record consolidated numbers: revenue of Rs 40,844 crore (+19.8% YoY), EBITDA of Rs 22,162 crore (54% margin), and PAT of Rs 13,832 crore (+34% YoY), with Q4 FY26 alone contributing Rs 13,544 crore revenue and Rs 5,033 crore PAT (+68% YoY) on a 60%+ operating margin. The balance sheet moved materially: debt-equity fell from 0.80x (Mar-25) to 0.36x (Mar-26) and net worth grew 70% to Rs 22,629 crore, funded by free cash flow of Rs 13,337 crore (pre growth-capex). Operationally the company remains genuinely best-in-class: zinc cost of production (ex-royalty) fell to a five-year low, averaging $959/tonne for FY26 (-9% YoY), which places HZL in the 1st decile of the global zinc cost curve -- a real structural moat that persists in both up- and down-cycles, unlike the earnings themselves. But the growth engine behind FY26 was overwhelmingly price, not volume: mined metal grew only ~2% YoY in Q4 and refined zinc ~6%, while LME zinc traded near $3,620/tonne in mid-July 2026 (a four-year high) on supply disruptions at Glencore's Kazzinc (Kazakhstan, post-explosion), Nexa's Cajamarquilla (Peru, post-fire) and Boliden's Garpenberg (seismic uncertainty) -- not a structural demand supercycle -- and Chinese refined output was already up 9.4% YoY in May, the normal supply response that historically erodes such spikes. Silver, at a record >$58/oz and by one analyst estimate ~44% of segment profit, contributed disproportionately too, even as HZL's own silver output fell 9% YoY in FY26 (627t vs 687t) on declining ore grades at Sindesar Khurd -- price fully offsetting a volume decline, the opposite of a healthy compounding story.

For FY27, management guides mined metal +3.2% YoY (~1,150kt), refined metal +4.9% (~1,100kt) and a silver recovery of +8.5% (~680t) -- credible given Q1 FY27's record 268kt mined output was explicitly attributed by management to 'better grades,' and given genuine capacity unlocks from Chanderiya/Dariba debottlenecking and the Debari roaster. Zinc cost of production is guided UP to $975-1,000/tonne (grade-driven cost creep as mines go deeper), and $500-600mn of FY27 growth capex (Hot Acid Leaching plant, fertilizer plant) is guided to be funded entirely from internal accruals -- a self-financing capex programme is a genuine positive, not funded by fresh leverage or dilution. The governance overlay is the second reason this stays off a high-conviction footing: Vedanta Ltd (promoter, ~60.7% post its Jan-2026 1.59% OFS) was forced to refund over Rs 1,030 crore of a disputed Rs 1,562 crore related-party 'brand and strategic services' fee routed to itself and onward to unlisted parent Vedanta Resources between FY23-FY25, after Viceroy Research flagged it as a regulatory/disclosure breach; the matter is still working through Supreme Court/ED scrutiny. Separately, the Government of India's residual ~27.9% stake (as of Mar-26) continues to be sold down in periodic tranches (1.6% in Nov-2025 for ~Rs 3,500 crore; further tranches reported and at other times denied through 2026) -- a recurring, uncalendarable overhang on the float, independent of HZL's own operating performance.

On a sourced back-of-envelope: FY26's trailing dividend (~Rs 21/share) against ~422.6 crore shares outstanding implies a payout of roughly Rs 8,874 crore, or ~64% of FY26 PAT -- well above the stated 30%-of-PAT policy floor. Combined with ~Rs 4,200-5,000 crore of FY27 growth capex, dividend-plus-capex is roughly equal to the entire Rs 13,337 crore pre-growth-capex FCF generated in FY26, leaving very little retained cushion if zinc or silver prices normalize down from today's cyclically elevated, largely supply-disruption-driven levels. Also note: Vedanta's own demerger (effective May 1, 2026; four new entities listed June 15, 2026) leaves HZL sitting inside the RESIDUAL Vedanta entity, whose value is now overwhelmingly a play on the ~63% (pre-dilution)/~60.7% (post-OFS) HZL stake -- this changes little for HZL minority holders directly but confirms HZL's cash flows remain the parent group's single most important lever.
recommendation_rationale: Hold, not Sell, because the two things that would justify selling out of a well-run structural franchise -- an obviously unsustainable valuation, or an unresolved balance-sheet/governance blow-up -- are not quite present. At ~15.9x trailing P/E (EPS Rs 32.74, price ~Rs 518) and a trailing dividend yield of roughly 4%, the stock is not priced at the kind of stretched multiple that would make a Sell automatic on valuation alone (contrast the 30-40x seen in some capex/defence-adjacent PSU names); and the brand-fee matter was at least partly self-corrected via a forced refund rather than left as an open wound. HZL's 1st-decile cost position is a genuine through-cycle asset -- it is what lets the company remain solidly profitable even if the current commodity tailwind (temporary mine-outage-driven zinc scarcity, macro-driven silver rally) fades, unlike higher-cost peers. But the same facts argue against adding exposure at current levels: FY26's growth was price-led not volume-led, cost of production is guided to rise (not fall) further in FY27, the payout-plus-capex programme leaves almost no FCF cushion against a commodity reversal, and both the parent's demonstrated appetite for cash extraction and the government's residual-stake overhang are structural, recurring frictions rather than one-off events. Net: hold a structurally advantaged, well-capitalised commodity name through a cycle that looks closer to its peak than its trough, but do not treat current levels as a reason to add.
summary: Hindustan Zinc had a record FY26 (revenue up ~20%, profit up 34%) on the back of near four-year-high zinc prices and record silver prices, not on meaningfully higher volumes -- its own mined and refined output grew only mid-single digits, and its silver output actually fell 9% on declining ore grades. The company remains one of the world's lowest-cost zinc producers and has sharply strengthened its balance sheet (debt-to-equity down from 0.80x to 0.36x in a year), and is guiding a further, capex-funded volume recovery in FY27, including a rebound in silver output. Set against that: nearly all of the company's free cash flow is currently being paid out as dividend or ploughed into growth capex, leaving little buffer if zinc and silver prices retrace from today's elevated, largely supply-disruption-driven levels; and the stock carries a persistent governance overhang from the Vedanta parent's cash needs (a disputed related-party brand-fee payment had to be partly refunded after regulatory scrutiny) and a still-unresolved, periodically-selling Government of India stake. At roughly 16x trailing earnings and a ~4% dividend yield, the valuation is not extreme, but it does not offer much margin of safety against a commodity-price normalization either. We rate it a Hold: a genuinely well-run, low-cost franchise, but not one to add to at a point that looks closer to the top of its earnings cycle than the bottom.
positive_para: The honest bull case: HZL sits in the 1st decile of the global zinc cost curve, with zinc cost of production (ex-royalty) at a five-year low of $959/tonne for FY26 -- a structural advantage that persists through commodity cycles, unlike the earnings themselves. The balance sheet has been transformed in a single year (debt-equity 0.80x to 0.36x, net worth up 70% to Rs 22,629 crore), giving genuine capacity to self-fund the next leg of growth: FY27 guidance is for mined metal +3.2%, refined metal +4.9% and, notably, a silver output recovery of +8.5% (to ~680 tonnes) after two years of grade-driven decline, backed by real, already-commissioning capacity (Chanderiya/Dariba debottlenecking, the Debari roaster) rather than a distant paper project. Growth capex of $500-600mn for FY27 (Hot Acid Leaching plant, fertilizer plant) is guided to be funded entirely from internal accruals, so the expansion does not require fresh leverage or dilution. Dividend policy (minimum 30% of PAT; actual trailing payout closer to 64%) gives a real income floor -- a trailing yield of roughly 4% -- that partially cushions any multiple compression.
negative_para: The honest bear case, and the one that matters most: FY26's headline growth was a price story, not a volume story. Mined metal output grew only ~2% YoY in Q4 FY26 and refined zinc ~6%, while the 19.8% full-year revenue growth and 34% PAT growth were driven overwhelmingly by zinc trading near a four-year high (~$3,620/tonne in mid-July 2026) and silver at record levels (>$58/oz, by one estimate ~44% of segment profit) -- and HZL's own silver volumes actually FELL 9% YoY in FY26 on declining ore grades at Sindesar Khurd, meaning price alone is masking a real operational headwind. Crucially, the current zinc price spike is substantially a supply-disruption story -- outages at Glencore's Kazzinc, Nexa's Cajamarquilla and Boliden's Garpenberg -- not a demand supercycle, and Chinese refined output was already climbing (+9.4% YoY in May), the normal supply response that historically erodes such spikes. Cost of production is guided UP, not down, for FY27 ($975-1,000/tonne vs $959 in FY26) as mines go deeper -- the cost-curve advantage is real but eroding at the margin, not improving. On capital allocation, a back-of-envelope on the trailing dividend (~Rs 21/share on ~422.6 crore shares) implies a payout of ~Rs 8,874 crore (~64% of FY26 PAT), which combined with ~Rs 4,200-5,000 crore of FY27 growth capex is roughly equal to the entire Rs 13,337 crore pre-growth-capex free cash flow generated in FY26 -- there is essentially no retained cushion if commodity prices normalize down. Layered on top is a genuine, not hypothetical, governance overhang: Vedanta was forced to refund over Rs 1,030 crore of a disputed Rs 1,562 crore related-party 'brand fee' after allegations first raised by short-seller Viceroy Research (whose characterization Vedanta and HZL management publicly reject) triggered an ED probe and Supreme Court scrutiny, evidencing the parent's willingness to extract cash from HZL by means that did not survive regulatory examination; and the Government of India's residual ~27.9% stake continues to be sold down in unpredictable tranches, a recurring source of stock overhang independent of operating performance. At ~16x trailing earnings on what looks like peak-cycle profitability, there is limited margin of safety if either zinc or silver mean-reverts even partway toward historical norms.
reverse_dcf_judgment: At ~Rs 518/share (~Rs 2,19,062 crore market cap) against FY26 EPS of Rs 32.74, HZL trades at ~15.9x trailing earnings and a ~4% trailing dividend yield -- a moderate, not stretched, multiple in absolute terms. But those trailing earnings were produced at a zinc price (~$3,620/tonne) near a four-year high driven mostly by temporary mine outages elsewhere, and at a record silver price (>$58/oz) that is a macro/precious-metals phenomenon HZL does not control and that by one estimate alone accounts for ~44% of segment profit. Normalize zinc back toward a more typical historical trading range and silver back off record highs, and reported earnings would compress meaningfully even before any volume effect -- per company sensitivity disclosures reported by analysts, roughly Rs 660-690 crore of EBITDA moves per $100/tonne of zinc and Rs 170-190 crore per $1/oz of silver, underscoring how much of FY26's profit pool is price rather than volume. The 15.9x multiple is therefore best read as the market implicitly extending a large chunk of today's cyclically elevated commodity backdrop into the near-term run-rate, while giving credit for the genuinely durable pieces -- the 1st-decile cost position and the de-levered balance sheet -- as a floor. That is a defensible, not a cheap, place to be: the multiple does not scream bubble the way a 30-40x cyclical name would, but it is not building in much margin of safety for mean reversion either. Through-cycle, on normalized commodity assumptions, HZL can plausibly clear a mid-teens multiple on the strength of its cost position and self-funded volume growth, but cannot easily justify a re-rating from here without either sustained commodity strength (which the supply-disruption-driven nature of the current zinc spike argues against extrapolating) or a step-change in volumes beyond what FY27 guidance already contemplates.
